en.title: Remove One Node to Stop Malware Spread
en.description:
Delete exactly one node together with its incident edges, then let the infection spread along undirected edges from the remaining initially infected nodes until no new node is infected. A healthy node may be deleted. Find the deletion that minimizes the final number of infected nodes, breaking ties by the smallest 1-based number.

The input/output format was compiled by this site.
en.input: The first line contains n m, the second line contains n initial infection flags, each 0/1, and then m lines follow with 1-based edges u v. 1≤n≤1000, 0≤m≤min(n(n−1)/2,1000); this site treats the graph as a simple undirected graph, with no duplicate edges and no self-loops.
en.output: Output the number of the node to delete. Even if there is no infection, one node must still be deleted.
en.explanation: The answers are 3, 1, and 3. In the third example, healthy node 3 is a cut vertex, and deleting it is better than deleting any single infection source. Original example 1 omitted node 1 from its spread set; the deletion answer 3 is unchanged.
hints: Enumerate every node as the deletion candidate, simulate the spread in the remaining graph with a multi-source BFS each time, and compare the final infected counts and node numbers.
